introduction: ReClass: Breakout is a memory-hacking game. You play ROOKIE, a maintenance robot breaking out of a memory-research facility. Rooms 0–9 are the main path; rooms 10–13 are an optional Advanced chapter. Each room teaches one ReClass technique, one step at a time. Steps tagged IN GAME happen in the game window, steps tagged IN RECLASS happen in ReClass, and each step says why it works and what you should see. A room only counts as complete when the game sees the result of your memory work, and completing it opens the next room.
find_rookie: Lost ROOKIE's class (new ReClass session or new game process)? Shoot once, then in the Scanner choose `Integer (4 Bytes)`, `Is Equal`, the ammo shown in the HUD, and `First Scan`. Shoot again, enter the new ammo and click `Next Scan`; repeat once more if several results remain. Right-click it → `Create class at address`, then add ` - 4` to the class address. Row 0000 changed to `Int32` reads ROOKIE's health.

lessons.title: Attach
lessons.goal: Connect ReClass to this game so it can read and write the game's memory.

steps.text: Start ReClass.NET (the x64 build for this platform).
Open `File` → `Attach to Process...`, select ReClassBreakout with the PID shown in this game's top bar, and attach.
steps.see: The ReClass title bar shows the game's process.

steps.text: Open `Process` → `Memory Searcher...`. This Scanner window is your main tool for the first rooms. Keep it open.
steps.see: The Scanner window, with First Scan and Next Scan buttons.

steps.text: Walk with WASD, aim with the mouse and click or press Space to shoot. Press E at glowing consoles. Tab hides this drawer. Finishing a room opens the next one.

lessons.learned: ReClass is attached. Every room from here on changes something inside this process.

explain.title: What ReClass actually does
explain.text:
Every number you see in a game (health, ammo, a timer, a position) is stored somewhere in the game's memory as a few bytes. ReClass is a tool that can look inside another running program's memory, show you those bytes, and change them while the program keeps running.

Attaching is you asking the operating system for permission to do that. Once ReClass is attached, the game never notices: from its point of view, its own numbers just changed by themselves.

explain.title: The plan for the whole game
explain.text:
Every room follows the same loop:

- Find: locate the value or code that matters.
- Understand: work out what it is and what sits around it.
- Change: edit it, and watch the game react.

Each room adds one new way to find or change things, and later rooms reuse what earlier rooms built.

explain.title: Your first tool: the Scanner
explain.text:
`Memory Searcher...` opens the Scanner. It searches all of the game's memory for a value and gives you a list of addresses that match. `First Scan` starts a new search; `Next Scan` only re-checks the addresses from the previous list. That second part is the whole trick, and Room 1 shows why.

> Watch the game window: whenever a value changes from outside the game, it flashes violet as MEMORY WRITE DETECTED. That's your edit landing.

lessons.title: Drone Swarm
lessons.goal: Shoot down all 20 drones. You only have 12 shots, and there is no way to reload.

steps.text: In the Scanner set Value Type `Integer (4 Bytes)`, Scan Type `Is Equal`, Value `12`, and click `First Scan`. Many addresses hold 12.
steps.why: Each scan remembers what it found; the next scan only checks those results again.
steps.see: Thousands of results: lots of memory happens to hold 12.

steps.text: Shoot one drone. Ammo drops to 11.
Set Value to `11` and click `Next Scan`. Only addresses that went 12 → 11 remain.
steps.see: Far fewer results. The more you repeat, the fewer remain.

steps.text: Shoot once more. Ammo drops by one again.
Set Value to the ammo shown in the HUD and click `Next Scan`. Keep going until one or two results remain.
Right-click the result → `Add selected results to address list`. In the list below, right-click it → `Change...`, enter `100` and confirm.
steps.see: MEMORY WRITE DETECTED: AMMO 10 → 100 in the game.

steps.text: Shoot the remaining drones.

lessons.learned: An exact-value scan plus a controlled change (shoot, value drops) narrows thousands of matches down to the one that matters.

explain.title: The big idea
explain.text:
You want ROOKIE's ammo, but memory is huge and the number 12 is everywhere: counters, sizes, colours, leftovers. A single search can't tell them apart. What can tell them apart is behaviour: only the real ammo drops to 11 when you shoot.

> Search, change the value in the game, search again for the new value. Each round keeps only the addresses that followed along.

explain.title: Why this works
explain.text: `First Scan` for 12 might give thousands of results. When you shoot and `Next Scan` for 11, ReClass checks only those thousands again. Unrelated 12s don't turn into 11 at the exact moment you fired, so they fall away. Usually one or two rounds is enough.

explain.title: Types matter
explain.text: Ammo is a whole number stored in 4 bytes, which ReClass calls `Integer (4 Bytes)`. If you searched for the same number as a `Float (4 Bytes)`, ReClass would compare different bit patterns and miss it. When a search finds nothing, the type is the first thing to check.

explain.title: Changing the value
explain.text: Once you have the address, writing 100 there changes the game's real state. The game doesn't keep a backup copy and it doesn't double-check: it simply reads ammo = 100 the next time you fire.

explain.title: In real games
explain.text:
This is the classic first move for money, health, ammo and score. Two common snags:

- The number shown on screen can be a separate display copy; editing that copy changes the text, not the real value.
- Some games store a value encoded (multiplied, offset or encrypted), so an exact search for the visible number finds nothing.

lessons.title: Cold Reactor
lessons.goal: Bring the reactor to 90% charge. The charge pad stops at 60%, and the gauge shows no number you could search for.

steps.text: Value Type `Float (4 Bytes)`, Scan Type `Is Between`, values `5` and `100`, then `First Scan`.
steps.why: You can't read the exact charge, but it's a percentage and the gauge isn't empty, so anything outside 5–100 can't be it. That one rule throws out millions of unrelated values.
steps.see: Many results. The next scans narrow them by how they change.

steps.text: Stand on the blue CHARGE pad for a second, then step off and stand still.
steps.see: The gauge rises.

steps.text: Scan Type `Has Increased`, `Next Scan`.
steps.why: Only values that went up since the last scan stay in the list.

steps.text: Stand on the red DRAIN vent for a second, then step off and stand still.
steps.see: The gauge falls.

steps.text: Scan Type `Has Decreased`, `Next Scan`. Then, without touching anything, `Has Not Changed` + `Next Scan`.
steps.why: Each round throws out values that didn't move the way the charge did.
steps.see: A handful of results with similar values.

steps.text: Add the result to the address list and `Change...` it to `95`. The gauge jumps.
steps.see: The gauge jumps past the gold mark.

steps.text: Press E at the reactor console.

lessons.learned: When you can't see a value, scan for how it changes: increased, decreased, unchanged.

explain.title: The big idea
explain.text: Here you can't see the exact number, only a bar. So instead of searching for a value, you search for how it behaves: it went up, it went down, it didn't change.

explain.title: Start with a sensible range
explain.text:
Charge is a percentage and the bar isn't empty, so the real value must be somewhere between 5 and 100. `Is Between` 5 and 100 throws out millions of values in one go. Much of what's left is the game's own graphics data, mostly colours stored as fractions between 0 and 1, which the range excludes.

> Before any relative scan, use what you know: the type, a plausible range, whether it can be negative.

explain.title: How the relative scans narrow it
explain.text:
- `Has Increased` keeps values that went up since the previous scan (you stood on the charge pad).
- `Has Decreased` keeps values that went down (you stood on the drain vent).
- `Has Not Changed` keeps values that stayed put (you stood still).

Each scan compares against the snapshot from the previous scan. So do the in-game action, stop, then scan. Don't scan while things are still moving.

explain.title: Why floats
explain.text: Smoothly changing values (charge, speed, positions, timers) are usually floating-point numbers: `Float (4 Bytes)`. Whole-number counters (ammo, money, kills) are usually integers.

explain.title: In real games
explain.text: Health bars without numbers, stamina, hidden reputation, cooldown timers: anything you can make go up and down on demand can be found this way.

lessons.title: Collapsing Bridge
lessons.goal: Cross the bridge before it collapses. At ROOKIE's speed of 60 the crossing takes 9.7 seconds and the bridge lasts 8. Speed never changes, so you can't scan for it: find ROOKIE's data through his ammo, then read speed off the structure.

steps.text: Shoot once (click anywhere in the room).
steps.why: Ammo is the easiest value to find: you can change it whenever you like.
steps.see: Ammo 11 in the HUD.

steps.text: In the Scanner: Value Type `Integer (4 Bytes)`, Scan Type `Is Equal`, Value `11`, `First Scan`.
steps.see: Many results: lots of memory happens to hold 11.

steps.text: Shoot once more.
steps.see: Ammo 10.

steps.text: Value `10`, `Next Scan`. If more than one result is left, shoot once more and `Next Scan` with the new ammo.
steps.see: One result left: ROOKIE's ammo.

steps.text: Right-click the result → `Create class at address`. Click the address at the top of the class, add ` - 0xC` to the end and press Enter.
steps.why: This shows you the 12 bytes stored just before your ammo. Fields of one character sit side by side, so the neighbours are other parts of ROOKIE.
steps.see: Rows 0000, 0008, 0010 and so on; your ammo is now in the second half of row 0008.

steps.text: Right-click row 0008 → `Change Type` → `Int32`.
steps.see: It reads 100, matching HP 100 in the HUD: health sits right before ammo. Row 0000 above it looks like random junk, so it isn't part of ROOKIE.

steps.text: In the Scanner, right-click your ammo result → `Create class at address` again, and this time add ` - 4` to the class address. Use this new class from now on.
steps.why: Health is the first value that belongs to ROOKIE, so his data starts 4 bytes before ammo. Room 6 will confirm it: the game itself points at exactly this address.
steps.see: A fresh class whose first 4 bytes are health and next 4 are ammo.

steps.text: Walk around for a few seconds while watching the class view in ReClass.
steps.why: ReClass colours a row red while its value is changing.
steps.see: Row 0010 flashes red as you move: that's X and Y. Row 0008 never flashes.

steps.text: Right-click row 0008 → `Change Type` → `Float`. It reads 60: that's speed. Double-click the value and enter `150`.
steps.why: An object's fields sit side by side in memory; speed lives right next to position.
steps.see: MEMORY WRITE DETECTED: SPEED 60 → 150.

steps.text: Click `Start run` (or press Enter), wait for GO, and run right to the exit.
steps.see: You reach the exit with time to spare.

lessons.learned: You don't need to scan for every value. Find one field you can change, open a class there, and read its neighbours. Keep this class: the next rooms use it.

explain.title: The big idea
explain.text: You can't scan for speed: it's always 60, so nothing filters it. Instead you find something you can change (ammo), and then look at the memory around it. Speed turns out to be right next door.

explain.title: How games store characters
explain.text:
Games are usually written in C++ or C#, where a character is a class or struct, something like:

```
struct Actor {
    int   health;   // +0x00
    int   ammo;     // +0x04
    float speed;    // +0x08
    float charge;   // +0x0C
    float x, y;     // +0x10, +0x14
};
```

The compiler lays those fields out one after another in one block of memory, and each character gets its own copy of that block. So once you find one value, the rest of that character is usually within a few hundred bytes of it.

explain.title: A ReClass class is your guess at that layout
explain.text: `Create class at address` opens a view of the memory starting at an address, as rows of bytes. You then tell ReClass what each row is (`Int32`, `Float`, `Pointer`...) and give it a name. You're writing down the game's struct by observation.

explain.title: Where does the object start?
explain.text:
Nothing in memory says "ROOKIE starts here". You work it out:

- Look a little before your ammo: right before it sits 100, matching HP 100 in the HUD. That's health.
- Before health, the values stop making sense as game data. So health is the first field, and the object starts at ammo - 4.
- Room 6 confirms it: the game itself points at exactly that address.

> An object usually starts at the first field that makes sense; the game's own pointers to it confirm the guess.

explain.title: Watching values change
explain.text: ReClass colours a row red while its value is changing. Walk around and the row holding X and Y flashes; the row holding speed never does. That's often the fastest way to label rows.

explain.title: In real games it's messier
explain.text:
- Big parts (inventory, weapon, stats) usually live in separate objects, with a pointer to them stored in the character. Room 5.
- C++ classes with virtual functions start with an 8-byte pointer to a function table, so real fields begin after it.
- The compiler adds padding gaps to align fields. Room 4.
- Enemies are often in a list or array: find one and the next is a fixed distance away or one pointer hop further.
- Some engines store all positions together and all health values together, instead of per character.
- Characters are created at runtime, so their address changes every launch. Room 6 solves that.

lessons.title: Blast Door
lessons.goal: The door needs a keycard (byte = 1), power on (flags bit 0) and alarm off (flags bit 1). It also checks the maintenance bit (bit 7), so don't wipe the other bits.

steps.text: In your ROOKIE class (lost it? see "Find ROOKIE again" below), right-click row 0018 → `Change Type` → `UInt32`.
steps.see: It reads 130. In binary that's 1000 0010: bit 7 (maintenance) and bit 1 (alarm) are on, bit 0 (power) is off.

steps.text: Press E at the ALARM switch.
steps.see: Row 0018 changes to 128: only the alarm bit turned off.

steps.text: Double-click the value and enter `129`.
steps.why: 129 = 128 + 1: keep bit 7, turn on bit 0 (power), leave bit 1 (alarm) off.
steps.see: The PWR and ALARM lights on the door panel turn green.

steps.text: Right-click row 0020 → `Change Type` → `UInt32` (that's clearance). A 4-byte row appears at 0024: right-click it → `Change Type` → `UInt8` and set it to `1`.
steps.why: The keycard is a single byte. Writing a 4-byte value there would also overwrite the bytes after it.
steps.see: The KEY light turns green.

steps.text: Press E at the door panel.
steps.see: The blast door slides open.

lessons.learned: Small fields share a word or sit in single bytes. Change only the bits you mean to change.

explain.title: The big idea
explain.text: Not every field is a full number. A yes/no value often takes a single byte, and several on/off switches are often packed into the bits of one number. Edit only the bits you mean to change.

explain.title: Reading flags as bits
explain.text:
The flags field reads 130. In binary that's 1000 0010:

- bit 1 (value 2) is the alarm.
- bit 7 (value 128) is maintenance mode, which the door also checks.
- bit 0 (value 1) is power, and it's off.

Flipping the alarm switch changes 130 to 128: only bit 1 cleared. That's how you confirm which bit means what: change one thing in the game and watch which bit moves.

explain.title: Why 129
explain.text:
You want power on, alarm off and maintenance kept: 128 + 1 = 129. Writing 1 instead would also clear the maintenance bit, and the door would refuse you.

> To set a bit, add its value; to clear it, subtract it. Never overwrite the whole number blindly.

explain.title: Single bytes and padding
explain.text: The keycard is one byte at 0x24. If you wrote a 4-byte number there, you'd also overwrite the next three bytes. Here those are padding, the gap the compiler leaves so the next field starts on an even boundary, but in real games they're often other fields.

explain.title: In real games
explain.text: Status effects, unlocked abilities, quest progress and permissions are very often bit flags. Changing the right bit unlocks one thing; changing the whole number can break several.

lessons.title: Armored Sentinels
lessons.goal: Each sentinel's armor needs a 20-damage hit and your weapon does 5. Upgrade it, and keep it upgraded after a swap hands you a brand-new weapon object.

steps.text: In your ROOKIE class, right-click row 0040 → `Change Type` → `Pointer`, then expand it with its arrow.
steps.why: Row 0040 holds an address, not a value: the inventory is a separate object.
steps.see: A nested class: ROOKIE's inventory.

steps.text: In the inventory, change row 0010 to `Pointer` and expand it.
steps.see: The equipped weapon. Its first bytes spell PULSE.

steps.text: In the weapon, change row 0018 to `Int32` (it reads 5: damage) and set it to `30`.
steps.see: MEMORY WRITE DETECTED: DAMAGE 5 → 30.

steps.text: Shoot sentinel A.
steps.see: ARMOR BREACHED: it goes down.

steps.text: Press E at the weapon rack.
steps.why: Swapping creates a brand-new weapon object somewhere else in memory.
steps.see: DMG 7 in the HUD: the upgrade is gone.

steps.text: Look at your class: the equipped pointer now leads to the new weapon. Set its damage (row 0018) to `30` again.
steps.why: A pointer row always follows the address stored right now, so your class found the new object by itself.

steps.text: Shoot sentinel B.
steps.see: Both sentinels down.

lessons.learned: Objects move; the pointers to them update. Follow pointers from a stable object instead of remembering addresses.

explain.title: The big idea
explain.text: Some fields don't hold a value; they hold the address of another object. That's a pointer. ROOKIE doesn't contain a weapon: ROOKIE points to an inventory, which points to the equipped weapon.

explain.title: Following the chain
explain.text: A pointer is just an 8-byte number that happens to be an address. Changing a row to `Pointer` tells ReClass to treat it that way and show you the object it points at, nested inside your class: ROOKIE → inventory → equipped weapon → damage.

explain.title: Why the upgrade disappeared
explain.text:
Swapping weapons creates a brand-new weapon object somewhere else in memory and stores its address in the equipped pointer. Your 30 damage was on the old object, which the game no longer uses.

> Objects come and go; the pointer to the current one is what stays put. Follow pointers from a stable object rather than saving the address of a temporary one.

explain.title: Why your class kept working
explain.text: A `Pointer` row in ReClass reads the address stored right now every time it redraws. After the swap it automatically showed the new weapon, so all you had to do was edit damage again.

explain.title: In real games
explain.text: Equipment, targets, the current vehicle, the local player inside a player list: almost everything interesting is reached through a chain of pointers. Mapping those chains in ReClass classes is the core of game reverse engineering.

lessons.title: Static Root
lessons.goal: The relay's control block moves to a new address every time it reboots. Power the relay door in 3 different control blocks by building a pointer path that always finds the current one.

steps.text: In your ROOKIE class, right-click the class header → `Copy Address`.
steps.why: Anything in memory that holds this address is a pointer to ROOKIE.

steps.text: Scanner: Value Type `Long (8 Bytes)`, tick `Is Hex`, paste the address as Value, `First Scan`.
steps.see: Only a few results.

steps.text: For each result: right-click → `Create class at address` and change its row 0018 to `Int32`. The control block is the one reading 6 (this room's number). Copy its address.
steps.see: One class reads 6 at row 0018.

steps.text: Scanner again: `Long (8 Bytes)`, `Is Hex`, Value = the control block's address, `First Scan`.
steps.see: One result is green: it lives inside the game's executable. Hover it to see <ReClassBreakout>+0x… .

steps.text: Set the control-block class address to `[<ReClassBreakout>+0xOFFSET]` with that offset (on Windows: `<ReClassBreakout.exe>`).
steps.why: Square brackets mean "read the pointer stored here". The executable's address is stable, so this always leads to the current block.

steps.text: In that class, change row 0020 to `Float` (relay power) and set it to `100`.
steps.see: The relay door opens: LINKS 1 / 3.

steps.text: Press E at the relay console to reboot it.
steps.see: The door shuts: the control block moved.

steps.text: Your class followed the green pointer to the new block. Set relay power to `100` again, reboot, and repeat once more.
steps.see: LINKS 3 / 3.

lessons.learned: A green pointer inside the module survives reallocations and restarts. A class at [<module>+offset] always finds the current object.

explain.title: The big idea
explain.text: Objects made while the game runs (on the heap) get a new address every launch, and sometimes every time they're rebuilt. But the game's executable is loaded as one block, and its global variables sit at a fixed distance from the start of that block. Find a global that points to your object, and you have a path that always works.

explain.title: Pointer scanning backwards
explain.text: Scanning for ROOKIE's address as a `Long (8 Bytes)` finds every place that stores a pointer to ROOKIE. One of them is inside the control block (row 0x18 reads 6, the room number). Scan again for the control block's address, and the result shown in green lives inside the executable itself: a static pointer.

explain.title: Module + offset
explain.text:
ASLR (address space layout randomization) loads the executable at a different base address every run, but the offset inside it never changes. `<ReClassBreakout>+0x…` means "the executable's base, plus this offset", which is the same in every run.

In a class address, square brackets mean "read the pointer stored here". So `[<ReClassBreakout>+0x…]` says: take the executable's current base, add the offset, read the pointer stored there, and show that object.

> Static pointer → current object, recomputed every time. That's why your class followed the relay to each new control block.

explain.title: This also proves Room 3's guess
explain.text: The control block points exactly at the address you picked as ROOKIE's start. That's how you confirm where an object begins.

explain.title: In real games
explain.text: Real paths are usually longer: [[[module+offset]+0x30]+0x18] and so on. This is what saved cheat tables and trainers are made of, and it's why they keep working after a restart (until a game update moves things).

lessons.title: Turret Nest
lessons.goal: Find the instruction that subtracts your health, replace it with NOPs so the turret can't hurt you, then put the original code back.

steps.text: In your ROOKIE class, change row 0000 to `Int32` (it reads health, 100). Right-click it → `Find out what writes to this address...` and accept the debugger prompt.
steps.why: ReClass will list every instruction that changes your health.
steps.see: An empty watch window.

steps.text: Step into the red zone until the turret hits you once, then step out.
steps.see: A row appears in the watch window.

steps.text: Select the row and click `Confirm next execution`.
steps.why: The first row can point just past the real instruction; confirming catches the exact one.

steps.text: Take one more hit.
steps.see: The row turns green: confirmed.

steps.text: Click `Inspect / edit`, then `NOP selection`, `Preview`, `Apply`.
steps.why: NOP means "do nothing": the instruction that subtracts 10 health is replaced.
steps.see: Preview shows sub dword [rax], 0xA turning into NOPs.

steps.text: Take 3 hits in the zone.
steps.see: Health doesn't move.

steps.text: Click `Restore original`.
steps.see: The editor shows the original instruction again.

steps.text: Take one more hit.
steps.see: It hurts again: -10.

lessons.learned: Editing code changes every future execution, not just one value. Always restore what you patch.
lessons.restore: Restore original (or Patches → Restore all) before leaving. Restart room never restores code.

explain.title: The big idea
explain.text: So far you've changed data. Now you change code: the instructions the game runs. Instead of resetting health after each hit, you stop the hit from subtracting anything at all.

explain.title: Finding the code that writes health
explain.text: `Find out what writes to this address...` sets a hardware watchpoint: the CPU itself reports every instruction that writes to that address. When the turret hits you, the instruction that subtracts 10 shows up in the list.

explain.title: Why confirm
explain.text: The CPU reports the write just after the instruction has finished, so the first row can point at the following instruction. `Confirm next execution` stops on the actual instruction the next time it runs, and the row turns green with its exact boundaries.

explain.title: NOP
explain.text:
`sub dword [rax], 0xA` means "subtract 10 from the number at the address in rax": your health. NOP is an instruction that does nothing. `NOP selection` replaces those bytes with NOPs, so the subtraction never happens.

> A code patch changes every future execution, for everything that runs that code. Data edits change one value once.

explain.title: Always restore
explain.text: Patched code stays patched until you `Restore original`. Restarting the room doesn't touch code, and a forgotten patch makes later rooms behave strangely.

explain.title: In real games
explain.text: God mode, infinite ammo and no-cooldown cheats are very often a single NOP or small instruction change at the place that writes the value.

lessons.title: Overclock
lessons.goal: Make every shot add ammo instead of using it, then restore normal behavior.

steps.text: In your ROOKIE class, change row 0000 to `Int32` if it isn't already. The 4-byte row after it, at 0004, is ammo: right-click it → `Find out what writes to this address...`.
Shoot once.
steps.see: A row appears in the watch window.

steps.text: Select the row → `Confirm next execution`.
Shoot once more.
steps.see: The row turns green.

steps.text: Click `Inspect / edit`. In the Assembly pane change `dec dword [rax]` to `inc dword [rax]`, then `Preview` and `Apply`.
steps.why: dec subtracts 1, inc adds 1. Both are 2 bytes, so the new instruction fits exactly.
steps.see: Preview: FF 08 becomes FF 00.

steps.text: Shoot 3 times.
steps.see: Ammo goes up with every shot.

steps.text: Click `Restore original`.
Shoot once.
steps.see: Ammo goes down again.

lessons.learned: Assembly and hex are two views of the same bytes. A same-size replacement can be patched in place.
lessons.restore: Restore original (or Patches → Restore all) before leaving.

explain.title: The big idea
explain.text: Instead of disabling an instruction, you change what it does. `dec dword [rax]` subtracts 1 from ammo; `inc dword [rax]` adds 1.

explain.title: Assembly and hex are the same thing
explain.text: The CPU runs bytes. Assembly is just a readable name for them: FF 08 is `dec dword [rax]` and FF 00 is `inc dword [rax]`. The editor shows both, so you can check that your change is exactly what you meant.

explain.title: Why the size has to fit
explain.text:
Both instructions are 2 bytes, so the new one fits exactly in place of the old one. A longer replacement would overwrite whatever instruction comes next and break the program; that's what hooks are for (Room 11).

> In-place patches must be the same size or smaller. Smaller is padded with NOPs.

explain.title: In real games
explain.text: Turning a subtract into an add, flipping a comparison, or changing a jump so a check always passes: these small in-place edits are the bread and butter of patching.

lessons.title: Biometric Gate
lessons.goal: The gate accepts one secret callsign with engineer clearance. Nobody tells you the name: read it out of the scanner's code.

steps.text: In your ROOKIE class, change row 0028 to `UTF8 Text`, then right-click it → `Find out what accesses this address...`.
steps.see: It reads ROOKIE. Rows appear straight away: the game's own drawing reads your name every frame.

steps.text: Stand on the SCAN PAD in front of the gate.
steps.see: SCANNING... above the pad.

steps.text: Find the row whose count only rises while you stand on the pad (step off and back on to compare). Select it → `Confirm next execution`, then `Inspect / edit`.
steps.see: Instructions including mov rcx, 0x5245454E49474E45.

steps.text: Write that number's bytes backwards: 45 4E 47 49 4E 45 45 52. Read them as ASCII letters.
steps.why: x64 stores numbers lowest byte first, so text hidden in a number reads backwards.
steps.see: E N G I N E E R. The code also checks [rax+0x20] (clearance) equals 2.

steps.text: Click `Stop` in the watch window. Double-click your callsign and enter `ENGINEER`.
Change row 0020 to `UInt32` and set it to `2`.
steps.see: Both gate lights turn green.

steps.text: Stand on the scan pad again.
steps.see: ID ACCEPTED: the gate opens. You're out.

lessons.learned: You escaped the facility. Code holds secrets too: an access watch shows which instruction reads your data, and the instructions around it show what it compares against. The Advanced rooms ahead are optional.

explain.title: The big idea
explain.text: Code doesn't only change data; it also reads and compares it. If you can find the code that reads your name, the instructions around it show exactly what it's comparing against, secret included.

explain.title: Reads, not writes
explain.text: `Find out what accesses this address...` lists every instruction that reads or writes the callsign. Lots of code reads it (the game draws your name every frame), so you look for the row whose count only rises while you stand on the scan pad: that's the gate's scanner.

explain.title: Reading text hidden in a number
explain.text:
The scanner compares your name against `0x5245454E49474E45`. Those 8 bytes are letters, but x64 stores numbers lowest byte first (little-endian), so in memory they're 45 4E 47 49 4E 45 45 52. As ASCII that's E N G I N E E R.

> When a number in code looks like 4x/5x/6x/7x bytes, try reading it backwards as text.

explain.title: The rest of the check
explain.text: The next instructions also check that the byte after the name is zero (the name must end there) and that clearance at +0x20 equals 2. Matching all of it is what opens the gate. You didn't patch anything: reading the code was enough.

explain.title: In real games
explain.text: Hidden passwords, unlock codes, difficulty checks and "is this a debug build" flags are all found this way: watch who reads the data, then read their comparisons.

lessons.title: Shared Machinery
lessons.goal: The press damages both you and the sentinel through one routine. Each hit carries a 4-digit override code in register r9, and only your hits carry the real one. Catch it, put it in your clearance, and submit it at the console.

steps.text: Right-click your health row (0000, `Int32`) → `Find out what writes to this address...`.
Stand on the PRESS plate until it hits you, then step off.
Select the row whose count rose with the hit → `Confirm next execution`.
Step on the plate again until it hits you.
Click `Find accessed addresses`. In the new window set Condition `mem32(rax + 0x1C) == 1` (faction 1 is the player), tick `Pause on match`, click `Apply condition`. Click `Stop` in the first window.
Step on the plate. The press hits the sentinel (ignored), then you: the game freezes because ReClass paused it.
Select the captured row and read r9 in the register details, for example 0x1A2B. Convert it to decimal (0x1A2B = 6699). Click `Stop`, then `Resume (F5)`.
Set ROOKIE's clearance (offset 0020, `UInt32`) to that decimal number.
Press E at the override console.

lessons.learned: A condition filters which executions you see; Pause on match lets you read registers at that exact moment.

explain.title: The big idea
explain.text: The same code often runs for many objects. The press uses one damage routine for you and for the sentinel. To learn something only about your calls, you filter the watch with a condition.

explain.title: Conditions
explain.text: `mem32(rax + 0x1C) == 1` reads the 4 bytes at rax + 0x1C (the faction field of whatever actor is being hit) and only matches when it's 1, the player. `Pause on match` freezes the whole game at that exact moment, so you can read the registers.

explain.title: Registers carry data
explain.text: Functions receive their inputs in CPU registers. Here the routine is given a 4-digit code in r9 along with each hit, and only your hits carry the real one. The register view shows hex, so 0x1A2B becomes 6699 in decimal.

explain.title: Why a patch here would hit both
explain.text:
Filtering a watch only changes what you see. If you NOP'd this routine, the sentinel would become invulnerable too. Code that should only affect one object needs a check inside it, which is the next room.

> Watches filter observations; they never limit what a patch affects.

lessons.title: Energy Siphon
lessons.goal: Make each of your shots heal you by 5 while still using ammo. The sentinel fires through the same code and must not heal anyone.

steps.text: Right-click your ammo row (0004) → `Find out what writes to this address...`.
Shoot the training wall once.
Select the row whose count rose with the shot → `Confirm next execution`.
Shoot once more.
Click `Inspect / edit`. Set Patch mode `Hook` and Hook semantics `Insert after`: your code runs right after the original dec.

Paste this into the Assembly pane. RAX points at ammo (Actor + 0x4), so faction is at [rax+0x18] and health at [rax-0x4]:
pushfq
cmp dword [rax + 0x18], 1
jne .done
add dword [rax - 0x4], 5
.done:
popfq
Click `Prepare hook`, look over the Change preview, then `Apply`.
Shoot: health +5, ammo −1. Wait for the sentinel to fire: nobody heals.
Click `Restore original`.
Shoot once: ammo drops, no heal.

lessons.learned: A hook adds code without overwriting it: the original instruction moves into a trampoline. Insert before runs your code first; Replace selection drops the original, so you must include it yourself.
lessons.restore: Restore original (or Patches → Restore all) before leaving.

explain.title: The big idea
explain.text: Sometimes you want to add behaviour, not just change one instruction. A hook replaces a few bytes with a jump to your own code, runs it, and jumps back.

explain.title: How a hook works
explain.text:
- The original instructions at the hook site are moved into a new block of memory (the trampoline).
- The hook site becomes a jump to that block.
- The block runs your code and the moved original instructions, then jumps back to just after the hook site.

`Insert after` runs the original `dec` first and then your code. `Insert before` runs your code first. `Replace selection` drops the original, so your code must include it.

explain.title: Your payload
explain.text: `cmp dword [rax + 0x18], 1` checks the faction of whoever is firing; `jne .done` skips the heal for anyone who isn't the player; `add dword [rax - 0x4], 5` adds 5 health. `pushfq`/`popfq` save and restore the CPU flags so the game never notices your comparison.

explain.title: In real games
explain.text: Hooks are how mods add features: logging, custom rules, conditional cheats that affect only the player. The same idea underlies most game modding frameworks.

lessons.title: Decision Vault
lessons.goal: The vault checks three things and won't say which one failed. Step through its code, trace it to a CSV, then fix the inputs.

steps.text: In your ROOKIE class, right-click the keycard row (offset 0024) → `Find out what accesses this address...`.
Press E at the vault console.
Select the row whose count rose when you pressed E (the vault's `cmp byte [rax+0x24], 1`; press E again if unsure), click `Confirm next execution`, then press E at the vault again.
Click `Find accessed addresses`, tick `Pause on match`, click `Apply condition`. `Stop` the first window.
Press E at the vault. The game freezes: ReClass paused it at the vault's first check.
Select the captured row and press `Step into (F11)` a few times. Watch which conditional jump goes to the rejection: keycard first, then clearance (must be 2), then the alarm bit.
Click `Trace selected thread`, keep the limits, click `Trace`, and save the CSV. It lists every executed instruction with registers before and after. Then `Resume (F5)` and `Stop` the watch.
Fix the inputs in your class: keycard (0x24) = 1, clearance (0x20) = 2, flags (0x18) = 0.
Press E at the vault.

lessons.learned: Stepping shows each decision as it happens; a trace records the whole path so you can compare runs.

explain.title: The big idea
explain.text: The vault checks three things and only says "denied". To see which check fails, you pause the game at the first check and step through the code one instruction at a time.

explain.title: Compare and jump
explain.text: Decisions in code are a compare (`cmp`) followed by a conditional jump. The compare sets CPU flags; the jump goes elsewhere if the condition holds. Stepping with `Step into (F11)` shows which jump sends you to the rejection.

explain.title: Traces
explain.text: A trace records every instruction one thread executes, with the registers before and after, and saves it as a CSV. Comparing a failing trace with a passing one is a powerful way to find what differs.

explain.title: In real games
explain.text: License checks, anti-cheat decisions and "can the player do this?" logic are understood this way: break on the decision, step, and read the branches.

lessons.title: Return Visit
lessons.goal: Save the Overclock patch so it can be re-applied in a fresh game process, where every address has changed.

steps.text: Find and confirm the ammo writer as in Overclock, click `Inspect / edit`, replace it with `inc dword [rax]` and click `Preview`.
Enter a Name, set Saved locator `Module + offset`, click `Save definition`, then `File` → `Save`. The * in the title disappears once saved.
`Apply`, shoot once to see ammo go up, then `Restore original`.
Quit the game (Ctrl+Q) and start it again: it reopens in this room with every address changed.
Attach to the new PID. Open `Debugger` → `Saved and active patches...`, select your definition, click `Preview` (it resolves the new address from module + offset), then `Apply`.
Shoot 3 times: ammo goes up.
Click `Restore original` in the Patches window.
Shoot once: ammo goes down.

lessons.learned: Absolute addresses die with the process. Module + offset (or a unique byte pattern) finds the same code in every new process.
lessons.restore: Restore original (or Patches → Restore all) before leaving.

explain.title: The big idea
explain.text: A patch made by absolute address only works in the process you made it in. To reuse it, you save where it is in a way that survives a restart.

explain.title: Module + offset and patterns
explain.text: `Module + offset` stores the patch as "this executable, this many bytes in", like the static pointer in Room 6. A `Module pattern` stores a unique sequence of bytes near the code and finds it again by searching. Patterns can survive small game updates that shift offsets.

explain.title: Why ReClass checks the executable
explain.text: The saved definition remembers which executable it was made for (by hash). A different build has different code, so applying an old patch blindly could corrupt it. ReClass refuses instead of guessing.

explain.title: In real games
explain.text: This is how trainers and saved cheat tables keep working across launches, and why they break after a game update.
